title: Chaupai Sahib
hook: a prayer asking to be kept under the Guru's protecting hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, the savaiya, ten verses ending in love. Your line was without love, nothing. Did anything impressive cross your screen that the savaiyas would have weighed differently? Day one hundred thirty-two.

A child is crossing a busy road. Halfway across, without looking up, the small hand reaches out, and a bigger hand closes around it. Nobody has to say anything. Grown-ups have their own versions of that moment: a diagnosis, a turbulent flight, a phone call at two in the morning. Sikhs have a prayer that is built around that reach. Some say it every day, and some say it again when they're afraid. Today, Chaupai Sahib.
screen: `A SMALL HAND REACHES OUT.` → `TURBULENCE, A 2 A.M. CALL.` → `A PRAYER FOR THE REACH.`

segments.voice: Chaupai Sahib is by Guru Gobind Singh, and it comes from the Dasam Granth. Its full name is often given as Benti Chaupai: benti means a humble request, and chaupai is the verse form, short lines grouped in fours. It's recited in the morning by Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem, it's part of the evening Rehras, and it's one of the banis read at the Amrit ceremony. And the whole of it is one long request: keep me. The opening, in paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand; may the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Let my mind stay at your feet; cherish me as your own. Then the prayer widens. It asks to be kept from enemies, from harm, from those who would do wrong. It praises the One who creates and sustains everything, who knows each heart from inside. And it returns again and again to that picture of the hand. What's striking is that it's a request at all. Its author was the tenth Guru, and Sikh tradition remembers the hardships of his life: his father's execution, and later the deaths of his sons. Yet the prayer has no swagger in it. It speaks as someone asking to be carried. Some people, hearing a prayer for protection, expect it to promise nothing bad will happen. Chaupai doesn't promise that. The Guru's own life didn't look like that. What it asks for is to be held, to be counted as one of God's own, whatever comes. That's the reach the child makes on the road. Not a guarantee. A hand.
screen: `BENTI — A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `GIVE ME YOUR HAND.` · `A GURU WHO KNEW DANGER.` · `NOT A PROMISE: A HAND.` · then, large: `KEEP ME.`

segments.voice: If you can, find Chaupai Sahib, in a gutka, online, or as a recording, and read or hear its opening lines. Let them be slow. If you can't, simply sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up. Think of one thing you're carrying right now that feels too heavy. If you pray, you can hold it up in the words of Chaupai's opening request: protect me, giving me your hand. If you don't, just let your open hands hold it for a while. The bell holds the time.
Chaupai Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh's prayer in four-line verses, asking to be kept under God's protecting hand.
Your line: keep me. Today, in one anxious moment, open your hand at your side, just slightly, and remember the reach. Day one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib as part of the morning banis and within Rehras in the evening, and some say it at times of fear, before travel or at a hospital bedside.

fork.setup: you're frightened: a hospital waiting room, bad news coming. what does Chaupai ask for?
options: a guarantee that everything turns out fine.
to be held by God's hand, as one of God's own.
fork.reveal: the prayer asks to be kept and cherished as God's own. tradition remembers its author losing his father and his sons; it's a hand, not a guarantee.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chaupai, a verse form of short lines grouped in fours.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer for safety.
what it means: a humble request to be held under God's protecting hand, from a Guru who knew real danger.
what a scholar hears: Benti Chaupai closes a long section of the Dasam Granth; the chaupai meter is four lines of sixteen beats each.
